item.title: CNMI gubernatorial, AG races still undecided
item.description: No winners have been declared in the 2026 CNMI runoff election as approximately 1,350 absentee ballots remain to be counted. According to updated unofficial results released Saturday by the Commonwealth Election Commission, the Republican gubernatorial ticket of Ralph DLG Torres and Benjamin Jones Jr. leads the race with 6,352 votes, or 53.1% of ballots cast.
item.content:encoded:
No winners have been declared in the 2026 CNMI runoff election as approximately 1,350 absentee ballots remain to be counted.

According to updated unofficial results released Saturday by the Commonwealth Election Commission, the Republican gubernatorial ticket of Ralph DLG Torres and Benjamin Jones Jr. leads the race with 6,352 votes, or 53.1% of ballots cast.

The independent team of Blas Jonathan Attao and Edmund Villagomez follows with 5,609 votes, or 46.9%.

In the attorney general race, Joaquin "Jack" DLG Torres has taken a narrow lead with 5,917 votes, or 50.3%, compared to 5,845 votes, or 49.7%, for Michael Evangelista.

The latest figures include ballots from Tinian, which were delayed Friday night due to rough seas and a high surf advisory that prevented election workers from transporting ballots to Saipan.

Before the Tinian votes were added to the tally, Evangelista held a 306-vote advantage over Torres. The additional ballots reversed that outcome and gave Torres a slim 72-vote lead.

Despite the updated count, the results remain unofficial until absentee ballots are canvassed and tabulated. Election officials expect that process to continue through Dec. 4.

The runoff was required after no gubernatorial and AG candidates received more than 50% of the vote in the Nov. 3 general election. Ralph Torres and Jones led that contest with 49.5% of the vote, while Attao and Villagomez finished second with 38.7%, advancing both tickets to the runoff.

While Joaquin Torres led in the Nov. 3 general election with 5,073 votes, or 39.7%, followed by Evangelista with 3,854 votes, or 30.2%.

item.title: Tax attorney: Investor interest growing in CNMI incentive programs
item.description: Tina Azarvand, managing partner of Azarvand Tax Law, said mainland investors are expressing growing interest in relocating businesses to the Northern Mariana Islands through the Commonwealth Economic Incentive Act and the Commonwealth Economic Development Authority's Qualifying Certificate program, though many are waiting to see how the newer incentive program is implemented. item.content:encoded:
Tina Azarvand, managing partner of Azarvand Tax Law, said mainland investors are expressing growing interest in relocating businesses to the Northern Mariana Islands through the Commonwealth Economic Incentive Act and the Commonwealth Economic Development Authority's Qualifying Certificate program, though many are waiting to see how the newer incentive program is implemented.

Azarvand said she has discussed CNMI investment opportunities with clients who initially sought information about Puerto Rico's tax incentives but became interested in exploring the commonwealth's programs.

"There is definitely interest in the CNMI," she said, noting that one prospective investor traveled from Florida to visit the islands and evaluate opportunities firsthand.

Among those expressing interest are two firms considering operations in the CNMI. One is involved in private equity with a broad range of investment interests, while the other focuses on service-based businesses that can operate remotely and export services outside the islands, she said.

Azarvand declined to identify the companies, saying discussions remain ongoing.

The firms initially viewed CEDA's QC program as their primary incentive option. The QC program provides qualifying businesses tax benefits in exchange for investments that support economic development in the CNMI.

They are now also evaluating opportunities under the economic incentive act, a recently enacted program aimed at attracting new investment and business relocation through additional tax-related benefits.

"They've kind of been wanting to see how this CEIA incentive program goes and see the viability for them as well," Azarvand said.

Azarvand said awareness of the CNMI's incentive programs remains limited among tax professionals on the mainland, including attorneys who specialize in Puerto Rico tax incentives.

"Most tax attorneys I speak with don't even know of the CNMI Qualifying Certificate program," she said.

She said that lack of awareness presents an opportunity for the CNMI to market its incentive programs more aggressively as officials seek to diversify the economy and attract new private-sector investment.

item.title: Federal judge rules against administration in American Samoa seabed mining lease
item.description: A federal judge in Hawaii has ruled in favor of environmental groups opposing a seabed mining lease sale in American Samoa, finding that the National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act when it approved the sale. The lease sale was set for Thursday, California time. The judge did not specifically issue an injunction canceling the sale, although the agency consultation was
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge in Hawaii has ruled in favor of environmental groups opposing a seabed mining lease sale in American Samoa, finding that the National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act when it approved the sale.

The lease sale was set for Thursday, California time. The judge did not specifically issue an injunction canceling the sale, although the agency consultation was voided.

Faʻasao Amerika Samoa and Conservation Council for Hawaiʻi, represented by the environmental law organization Earthjustice, filed a lawsuit after the National Marine Fisheries Service determined that the Marine Minerals Administration lease sale was not likely to adversely affect endangered species.

The court ruled that the Fisheries Service accepted the administration’s definition of the “agency action” as the lease sale itself, not post-lease activity.

“By doing so, [National Marine Fisheries Service] only considered the preliminary effects of the lease sale and did not even attempt to consider potential effects of post-leasing activities. NMFS’s cramped, expedited, informal consultation is apparently unprecedented in the context of leasing on the [Outer Continental Shelf],” the ruling stated.

In a news release Wednesday, Earthjustice said the ruling was a win for the people of American Samoa, “as well as the whales, sharks, and sea turtles who call the waters surrounding these islands home.”

“It recognizes that the law requires the government to understand the full repercussions of its actions before letting this untested industry destroy one of the most pristine parts of the ocean on the planet,” said Chris Eaton, Earthjustice attorney.

Last year, the Trump administration vowed to fast-track seabed mining to give the United States access to critical minerals deep in the ocean.

A lease sale for up to 69 million acres east and west of the Mariana Islands is set for Dec. 16. The American Samoa and Mariana Islands leases involve areas within the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone.

On Tuesday morning, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration held a virtual public hearing on an application from a company that wants to look for polymetallic nodules in international waters.

Eco Minerals, previously known as Deep Sea Rare Minerals, wants to explore an area of seabed about 700 miles east-northeast of Guam, as well as eight areas in the Eastern Pacific’s Clarion-Clipperton Zone.

Those who testified in the hearing urged regulators to deny the license, arguing that the deep-sea ecosystem is not well understood and mining could cause long-term harm.

item.title: Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions
item.description: The agrochemical and biotech giant Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company alleging the weed-killer Roundup caused their cancer. On Friday, a judge in Missouri gave final approval to the nationwide settlement that could cost the company up to $7.25 billion in the coming years.
item.content:encoded:
The agrochemical and biotech giant Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company alleging the weed-killer Roundup caused their cancer.

On Friday, a judge in Missouri gave final approval to the nationwide settlement that could cost the company up to $7.25 billion in the coming years.

The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma — a blood cancer that they claim is linked to glyphosate, which is the main ingredient in Roundup.

Under the settlement in circuit court, people affected could receive anywhere from $10,000 to $165,000 in compensation, depending on whether their work in agriculture or other occupations exposed them to higher levels of glyphosate, the age when they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and other factors.

In a statement , the CEO of Bayer, Bill Anderson, called the settlement a "decisive milestone" that will "mitigate the risks" of pending and future litigation.

The presiding judge, Timothy Boyer, said it was "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."

Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favor of Bayer, the German company that now owns Monsanto, finding that it could be shielded from lawsuits filed in state courts over claims that it failed to warn consumers about the cancer-causing effects of glyphosate.

Roundup is the most widely used weed-killer in the world.

The attorney representing the plaintiffs, Christopher Seeger, said in a statement that "Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice."

The latest settlement comes in addition to a previous one in which Bayer agreed to pay between about $10 billion and $11 billion to settle more than 100,000 claims related to Roundup.

More than a decade ago, the World Health Organization's cancer agency concluded that glyphosate is probably carcinogenic to humans. Prominent scientists in the field of environmental health have echoed those concerns as recently as this year.

But Bayer has steadfastly denied that its product causes cancer.

The Environmental Protection Agency has also concluded it "did not identify risks of concern from glyphosate uses, including for cancer," though the agency is currently conducting a review of the evidence related to human health after facing intense pressure from advocates and some scientists.

Concerns about the safety of glyphosate has been an animating issue for supporters of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr and his Make America Healthy Again agenda.

However, the Trump administration has taken steps to support the herbicide-maker, siding with Bayer in the Supreme Court case and issuing an executive order to promote domestic production of glyphosate.

Several years ago, the company removed glyphosate from its U.S. products used in residential settings, although it's still in use in the agricultural industry.

item.title: Storms expected on both coasts threatens Thanksgiving travel
item.description: Before worrying about the temperature of the turkey, travelers could face a different type of uncertainty next week. This time , it's the weather — and it's affecting both U.S. coasts. "I know there's a lot of travel for many of you as you head into the Thanksgiving holiday, but I'm going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential," said San Francisco Mayor Daniel L
item.content:encoded:
Before worrying about the temperature of the turkey, travelers could face a different type of uncertainty next week. This time , it's the weather — and it's affecting both U.S. coasts.

"I know there's a lot of travel for many of you as you head into the Thanksgiving holiday, but I'm going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential," said San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie on X Friday . He said the city is preparing this weekend for extreme high tides and rain that could hit the area Monday afternoon through Wednesday.

Over the past week, cities in California saw mudslides, waterspouts and flooding while Florida also saw coastal flooding and inundated streets. A new set of storms are expected to hit both sides of the country early next week, just as travelers head into the holiday week.

It's already been a wet fall in large swaths of the country, thanks in part to a Super El Niño , a natural climate pattern that shifts weather around the world. Devastating flooding in the Southwest U.S. left multiple people dead and hundreds stranded, and California and the Pacific Northwest have seen high sea level and multiple strong atmospheric rivers .

"Take this weekend: get yourself ready," Lurie, the San Francisco mayor, said after a call with the National Weather Service and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Rain and snow, in higher elevations, is possible over parts of the northwest and northern California on Saturday, according to the NWS .

The West Coast is forecasted to see an atmospheric river, a narrow band of water vapor pushed by the wind, on Monday. Another is expected for the Pacific Northwest later in the week, according to the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes . Atmospheric rivers hang over an area and dump precipitation. They can cause months worth of rain in just a few days.

The center expects two to four inches of precipitation over northern California and southern Oregon through Wednesday.

Coastal flood advisories are also in effect through Monday morning in the Bay Area, the NWS said. This comes on top of historic high tides , known as King tides.

A storm that started in Florida Friday will move north to the Mid-Atlantic and into the Northeast by Sunday evening, according to the NWS .

Some of the heaviest rain could be seen on the coast of the Carolinas through Sunday morning. Then, heavy rain is expected to move up the coast, said Dan Hoffman, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Baltimore, Md.

Hoffman said during a busy travel week, even with the weather not expected to bring flooding or strong winds, it "doesn't usually take too much to cause things to start to have delays."

As for New England, Andrew Loconto, a meteorologist at the NWS in Norton, Mass., said the storm this weekend is not forecasted to be as big as another storm hitting the region after Thanksgiving. "That could be more impacts for people coming back home," Loconto said, pointing to another highly anticipated day across the U.S. — Black Friday.

item.title: Mexico detains top cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro,' setting off violence
item.description: MEXICO CITY — Gunfire rang out, trucks burned and Mexican forces clashed with cartel gunmen in the state of Sinaloa overnight as Mexican authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro." Meza Flores was one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives and a top cartel leader from the Beltrán Leyva criminal organization wanted for trafficking drugs to the United State
item.content:encoded:
MEXICO CITY — Gunfire rang out, trucks burned and Mexican forces clashed with cartel gunmen in the state of Sinaloa overnight as Mexican authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro."

Meza Flores was one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives and a top cartel leader from the Beltrán Leyva criminal organization wanted for trafficking drugs to the United States and illegally carrying firearms.

Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.

He was also a key ally to "Los Mayos," a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.

Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups.

But experts warn that it could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions.

Mexican authorities said they used "stealth and surprise" to capture Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him. He was later taken by aircraft to Mexico City to appear before prosecutors.

Video shared by authorities shows heavily armed men in camouflage escorting a man through a dimly lit house and putting him in the back of a truck. No casualties have been reported so far as a result of the operation.

The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence overnight with calm setting in Saturday morning.

Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders.

As a result, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to discuss the case.

"Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary," the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least "10 roadblocks" with burning vehicles on Guasave's streets.

Guasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations.

"Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks," Sánchez told The Associated Press.

She said that the city's firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning.

"Everything looks calm today," Sánchez said.

Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians.

Meza Flores' detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.

The U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities.

"The capture of El Chapo Isidro delivers a significant blow to a ruthless criminal organization that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities," the DEA said in a statement. "This operation underscores the critical importance of intelligence sharing in targeting dangerous cartel leaders."

García Harfuch called the detention "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa."

Sheinbaum's government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho," who was killed by the military in February.

Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy, which critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run.

The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa.

"What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States," Saucedo said. "What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don't dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact."

item.title: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
item.description: GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots." After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.
item.content:encoded:
GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."

After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.

Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.

Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo .

Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan , 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.

Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.

"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."

No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.

On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.

Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.

The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.

A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.

"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."

There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.

"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."

But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.

Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.
